We shall encounter another striking example later. Its meaning here becomes clearer still when, at this point in the tale, we see the Imam slip his hand beneath his robe and draw out Solomon's very seal, adorned with a red hyacinth, to show his astonished companions.

From now on the Imam will appear as a figure of the Logos, a cosmic reality present to every form of being and sustaining its existence. Two episodes immediately following this scene, with a magnificent vision between them, help us understand this. They mark the visionary travellers' entry into the malakût of the plant kingdom and the malakût of organic life.

In the first episode (I am considerably shortening the account here, although no explanation can replace the power of its visionary imagination), the wind carries the White Cloud and its travellers “to a mountain rising to a dizzying height. At its summit stood a great tree, drying up, its leaves falling one by one. ‘What is this tree?’ the companions asked.” The Imam replied, “Ask it, and it will tell you itself.”

But the tree speaks only when the Imam himself commands it, telling the companions that he used to come beneath its shade to celebrate the divine praise. For forty nights now the Imam has stayed away, and the tree is wasting with grief at his absence: it lives by the Imam's fragrance and the sight of him. At that very moment the Imam lays his hand upon the tree. To the companions' amazement it becomes green again, covered in flowers and fruit (§§ 11–13).

What does this apparition reveal? What secret lies in the Imam's gesture? The essential points of Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary are these. The high mountain is how the Earth's malakût appears, because a mountain is what holds things firm, and the Malakût makes the visible world, the molk, firm and supports it. The mountain is therefore the Earth's imaginal metaphysical reality as it appears in the Malakût, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world.

The great tree is the manifestation of the Angel or Logos (Kalima) entrusted with the growth of everything that sprouts on the earth and from it: the whole world of plants. The governing idea is this: the Malakût is the realm of life that never dies, and what pours out and transmits this life is a cosmic liturgy.

A familiar saying sums it up: each time you offer a doxology (tasbîh), you plant a tree in paradise. The heavenly worship of the beings of the Malakût fertilizes the realities of the visible world entrusted to their care and makes them flourish. Each higher level of being performs a liturgy that transmits life to the level below it.

Thus the Angel of the Earth receives his life from the liturgy the Imam performs beneath his shade. Between these acts of worship the tree does not die—nothing dies in the Malakût—but it dries up as it waits to become green again when the cycle of cosmic worship returns the Imam to its shade.

Qâzî Sa'îd believes that philosophers express this same liturgical outpouring of life in their hierarchy of Intelligences, from the Nous, or Intelligence of the universe, down to what they call the “Active Intelligence,” the Angel of the human race (identified by theologians as the Holy Spirit or Angel Gabriel).

Our visionaries hear the great tree speak because every being in the Malakût speaks through the soul within it, and the speech of that soul is its prayer or praise of God. When the tree speaks of the Imam's fragrance and the sight of him, it expresses its longing to receive the life that the Imam, as light and source of life, pours upon it.

A magnificent vision unfolds between this episode and the next. The Imam takes his place again on the White Cloud and commands the wind to carry him away. “And the wind lifted us so high that the surface of the earth appeared no larger than a shield. In the Air [that is, in the space of the Malakût] we saw an Angel whose head touched the sun and whose feet rested on the floor of the sea. Of his two outspread wings, one reached the East and the other the West.

“As we passed, we heard him utter the threefold shahâdat [testimony to the One, the Prophet and the Imam]” (§ 14). This towering figure is the Angel of the malakût of the element Air, in other words, the Angel of the space of the Malakût. (Later we shall learn that he is the one known in the fourfold company of archangels as Seraphiel.) Qâzî Sa'îd has tried elsewhere, in his metaphysics of time and space, to explain the immense proportions of such an appearance. That metaphysics shows that, when we speak of enfolding, it is equally correct to speak of an expansion of time and space.

When both are enfolded within the presence of the contemplating witness, the witness, in turn, becomes present to all of time and all of space. The Imam explains to his companions: “It is I who, by God's permission, caused this Angel to stand forth. I entrusted to him the darkness of Night and the brightness of Day, and so it shall remain until the day of Resurrection” (§ 15).

What the Angel spanning every horizon reveals, then, is the totality of times and places. Every past and every future, every “east” and every “west,” is present at once, gathered into the Angel's Image as it appears to the Imam and his companions. This is possible because the dimensions of that total Image correspond to what their malakûtî bodies, through their subtle faculty of vision, can perceive.

In the second episode surrounding that great vision, our pilgrims reach another lofty mountain near the famous wall Alexander raised against Gog and Magog (Yâjûj and Mâjûj). “The mountain was entirely black, as though it were a piece of night, and vapour rose from it” (§ 16). In the outward, literal sense, Gog and Magog (Quran 18:93) refers to certain peoples of Central Asia at the edge of the known world, against whom Alexander was said to have built a wall or embankment.

Esoterically, something quite different is meant. We are at the boundary where the malakût of the plant world ends and that of the animal kingdom begins: the realm of everything possessing the vital breath, or pneuma, made up of a vapour of its own kind. We are still at the level of a lower malakût, where subhuman souls, satanic souls and the souls of demons with human faces remain captive at the level of animal life, unable to rise toward the higher heavens of the Malakût.

The ascent toward the malakût of genuinely human reality will be experienced as a journey all around the mountain of Qâf and up to its summit. Here again we shall see what follows when time and space are enfolded or expanded to match the subtle organ of visionary perception—that is, to match human reality at the level of the Malakût.

I. The Three Thirds of the Night. — “Then the Imam said to the wind: ‘Take us to the mountain of Qâf.’ The wind carried us to the mountain of emerald, or green hyacinth, which encircles the world. An Angel rules over it, having a perfect human form; he is charged with governing that mountain.” As soon as the Angel has greeted the Imam, the Imam grants his wish by asking him to visit the mysterious prophet Khezr (§ 17).

We shall understand the meaning of this last detail a little later. For now, let us note that we have reached the third great stage of the visionary journey. In reaching the mountain of Qâf, the pilgrims reach the malakût of the human being, which itself comprises three levels.

The mountain of Qâf is well known throughout the visionary geography of Islamic theosophy. It is at once a cosmic and a psycho-cosmic mountain, and in both respects its characteristic colour is green. As the mountain encircling our world like a dome and marking the boundary between our world of becoming and the world of the Malakût, it is sometimes said to be made of emerald, sometimes to bear an emerald rock at the crown of its vault.

In either case, the visio smaragdina, the emerald vision, tells us that this mountain is one of the realities of the Malakût close to our world, the Molk. As such, it is a bodily reality, but in a subtle state, governed by a holy Spirit.

Considered as a psycho-cosmic mountain, it recalls for Qâzî Sa'îd the agreement among the Gnostics that green symbolizes the Orient where the light of the Spirit rises over the body. And since the Angel who rules the mountain has a perfect human form and governs the malakût of humanity, Qâzî Sa'îd calls him the Angel of the human race, the Angel of humanity (Rabb al-nû' al-insânî). This is the very designation found in Sohrawardî's “Oriental Theosophy.”

Salmân the Pure continues his story. Our pilgrims first reach the lowest level of the human malakût: the malakût of the vegetative life within us. That is why, just as at the first stage, they find themselves before a great tree whose leaves are drying up. This tree, however—speaking, as we have already learned that everything with a soul speaks through its soul—tells them how serious its plight has become: “I used to take pride in raising myself above the other trees. Now the other trees take pride in raising themselves above me.

“For the Imam used to visit me every night, during the first third of the night. He would remain in my shade for an hour. Then a black horse would come to him. He would mount it and ride away. I shall not see him again until his appointed hour, though I used to live by his fragrance and take pride in his presence. For forty nights now he has abandoned me. His absence has plunged me into sadness and grief, and I have become what you see before you” (§ 18).

Without our commentator's help, the tree's words would probably remain an enigma. The essential point is this: everything in the celestial world of the Malakût corresponds to a reality in earthly humanity, in nâsût. Now the human being as we know it here has three states: the vegetative state that allows the body to grow; the state of an animate, living creature; and the state of a thinking being.

The hierarchy of these three states must recur in the Image of humanity as it appears from world to world, beginning with the Malakût. Necessarily, then, the first thing to appear there is the vegetative level: the malakût of the activity that sustains growth and nourishment. Our commentator tells us that the tree is the visible manifestation of the malakûtî Angel or Logos with a Michaelic function (Kalima malakûtîya mîkâ'îlîya).

No doubt this is because, within the supreme fourfold order of archangels, Michael is responsible for providing the sustenance by which beings continue to exist. As for the tree's withering, we must again recall the liturgical mystery linking the worlds. Its plight is more serious here because humanity is more acutely conscious of its own shortcomings and suffers more keenly from the Imam's absence.
But that is also why the tree—which represents the malakût of vegetative life inherent in the human essence—once took pride in being above the other trees.

What is called Night here signifies both the absence of light and the capacity to receive the influx of the Lights of the Malakût. The Imam's coming, therefore—the coming of the very source of those Lights, the treasury of the secrets of a cosmic walâyat—must take place in the night of Matter's capacity for receiving what it awaits: its Light. Why does it happen during the “first third of the night”? Because this Night, the receptive capacity of humanity's subtle organism (isti'dâd al-latîfat al-insânîya), is divided into three thirds corresponding to the three levels of the human malakût.

The first belongs to the vegetative element in humanity, the second to animate life, and the third to the thinking nature (vis intellectiva, qowwat 'aqlîya). “That is why,” Qâzî Sa'îd counsels, “you should conscientiously fulfil the requirements of the liturgy of the last third. For that final third of the night is close to the day when the sun of True Reality rises over the human horizon.”

The black horse that comes to the Imam at the beginning of the second third of the Night is the luminous metaphysical reality, or Idea (haqîqat nûrîya), of the species of living creatures (nu' al-hayawân, the “animal”). It appears black—a black light—because the Source of Life is found in darkness. Its arrival beside the tree shows that the tree is rooted in animate life and is governed by the lord of life. The human being is a celestial “animate plant,” a “plant-animal” (nàbât samâwî hayawânî).

The perfection the Imam pours into this plant therefore passes through the Idea, the metaphysical reality of animate life (bi-tawassot al-haqîqat al-hayawânîya). The three human natures—vegetative, animate and thinking—are thus brought together in a single image: a rider mounted on a black horse beneath a great green tree. Having cared for the malakûtî plant through his liturgy, the Imam mounts the horse to attend to the education of animate life. Our commentator sums it up: “The first stage is the physical human being (insân tahî'î), the plant of the Malakût (nabât malakûtî).
“The second is the psychic human being (insân nafsî), the living creature of the Malakût (hayawân malakûtî).

“The third is the intellective human being (insân 'aqlî), the divine human being (insân ilâhî). The words ‘I shall not see him again until his appointed hour’ mean: until the fixed time each night, namely the first third. The Imam's nightly visit to the human vegetative principle in its subtle state within the Malakût lasts until the end of the first third, until it is interrupted for forty nights.” Here, as before, the Imam lays his hand upon the tree, “and behold, the tree became green again and was covered with leaves. We sat beneath its shade. Its greenery shone resplendently” (§ 19).

We may now begin to understand the secret meeting between the Angel of the human race and the mysterious prophet Khezr (Khadir), counterpart or companion of the prophet Elijah. Khezr initiates those who have had no human teacher and is always encountered near the Spring of Life. The Imam's companions, too, wonder about this meeting and ask what it means (§ 20). I can retain here only one aspect of our commentator's explanation.

In Avicenna's system, the last Intelligence in the cherubic hierarchy receives the influx of the higher Intelligences and passes it on to human souls. Here, the Angel governing the mountain of Qâf—the malakût of humanity, the Angel of the human race, who is the human Form of the divine Logos for the human world—receives light and spiritual influx from the Imam-Logos of the worlds, God's vicegerent (Khalîfat Allah), sovereign over all the lords or Angels of the species (compare Philo's ἀρχὴ τῶν ἀγγέλων).

The influx received by this Angel overflows from him. He must transmit it to the source from which it will branch out through the entire territory of his kingdom. For this Angel, that is what it means to be established upon his Throne, and that is what his meeting with Khezr signifies.
A short analysis by Qâzî Sa'îd makes this clear. The Malakût surrounds the molk, because spiritual substance surrounds bodily substance, not the other way around.

Hence the exodus from the bodily world, following the traces of the soul, is always described as a journey or descent into the region of darkness: a passage through the density of the material world until one emerges into the Malakût and the emerald vision, the visio smaragdina. The first sign of the soul is like the dampness encountered by someone digging a well. A second sign comes when water is reached. The first degree is the sight of water.

Then comes “the contact of water with the limbs, until one plunges into it and is completely immersed, so that the fish which is one's body disappears into that water. It is as though one had become the water itself. Such a person has truly reached the Spring of Life.” This was the exemplary experience of the prophet Khezr. “He cast the fish of his body into the Spring of Life, that is, into the ocean of the world of Spirits, so that his fish disappeared [an allusion to Quran 18:60], his body was effaced, absorbed into the Spirit. His was a body made spiritual, whereas other individuals are Spirits made bodily.”

That is why Khezr is the Throne of the Angel of humanity (of the Kalima, or divine Logos, set over the human species): through Khezr the life of the Malakût is maintained and spread throughout the Angel's kingdom, through all who learn from Khezr's example how to reach the Spring of Life (commentary on § 17). This is one of the first secrets of the mountain of Qâf.

II. Intermezzo. — At this point comes an interlude: the Imam's companions ask a question that would naturally occur to a Shiite Gnostic. Their extraordinary journey allows them to behold the Imam in his metaphysical reality within the Malakût, transfigured into the pure theophanic light of a caro spiritualis, a spiritual body. They learn that he has always existed, and always exists, in the Malakût.

What is the relationship between this divine person of the Imam (his lâhût) at the level of the supersensible worlds—his inner reality—and the purely outward appearance they had seen until now in the Imam's earthly, historical humanity? This relationship between the Imam's lâhût and nâsût corresponds term for term to the relationship, in Christology, between the eternally pre-existent Logos Christos and the flesh-and-blood man Jesus of Nazareth, who appeared for a brief interval in history.

So the companions ask the Imam: “Were you not with us in your dwelling? Then when were you on the mountain of Qâf?” The Imam answers: “Close your eyes.” We closed them. Then he said: “Open them.” We opened them, and behold, we were in Medina, and no one noticed us [that is, noticed our arrival from the Malakût].

“So here we are in Medina,” the Imam said, “without anyone being aware of us. Well, in the same way I am on the mountain of Qâf without any of you being aware of me [that is, being aware that I am there]. I swear by God! If you could see with your own eyes what I possess of the Malakût, you would cry: ‘Anta anta’ [‘You are you’: you are the absolute Subject, needing nothing beyond yourself to be yourself].
“Yet I am a servant of God, one creature among His creatures. I am someone who eats and drinks” (§ 21).

This already reminds us that, however exalted the Imam-Logos becomes in Shiite theosophy, it remains within the limits observed elsewhere by the Christology of Arius: the Logos is the first and highest of created beings. Before explaining the Imam's concluding declaration, however, our commentator turns to the companions' question: “We were with you in Medina. We knew everything concerning you. We saw you with us in the mosque and elsewhere.

“We cannot see when you could have gone to the mountain of Qâf.” In reply, the Imam tells them to close and then open their eyes. They find themselves in Medina, which they had never left bodily; yet they no longer see themselves there quite as they did before. For they grasp that, while they are in Medina, they are also on the mountain of Qâf, and no one around them notices.

The companions must understand: through the light of walâyat and their perfect receptivity, they have become people of the Malakût, “persons of light.” Qâzî Sa'îd here reminds the reader of his metaphysical premises. At their respective levels, movement, time and space correspond to one another, just as the boundaries of the worlds correspond. The subtler the space, the subtler its movement and time.

The malakûtî body is perfectly subtle and luminous; neither curtain nor barrier can conceal anything from it; neither earth nor heaven obstructs it. Such is the condition of Angels when they descend upon the prophets. The persons of the Malakût (ashkhâs malakûtîya) are not bound to one place in perceptible space rather than another: all places are equally open to them, all on the same footing.

So too with time and movement in the Malakût: they are so subtle that the times and movements of “our” world are enfolded within them, so that a mere fragment of malakûtî time and movement equals months and years of time in our world. By the time of the Malakût, the distance from the Ninth Heaven to the centre of the Earth is no more than the blink of an eye.

What, then, is the inner meaning of the command to close and then open their eyes? To close them, Qâzî Sa'îd explains, means here to close them to their presence upon the mountain of Qâf, whose wonders they are contemplating. When the soul turns toward one thing, contemplating it prevents the soul from contemplating something else, so long as its contemplation remains at the level of the heart.

Indeed, it belongs to the soul's very nature that, when it turns toward something, it becomes that very thing, provided its movement toward it answers an essential, ardent longing—a longing rooted in its own nature. Opening the eyes, on the other hand, alludes here to the companions' return to their selves of light (ilâ dhawâtî-him al-nûrîya), to seeing things through inward vision, through malakûtî eyes.

“Just as, for the malakûtî gaze, pre-eternity and post-eternity (azal wa abad) embrace one another in a perpetual nunc [now], so for those who possess this gaze the easts and the wests meet and join together.” For such people, therefore, circling the mountain of Qâf does not in the least exclude being in Medina at the same time. In an instant they grasp that they are in Medina, but in a way different from that of the people around them, who cannot perceive that the Imam's companions are on the mountain of Qâf.

“My friend!” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “if you look with this gaze, then most of the things you at first judged impossible you will now see reflecting their realities upon one another in this perspective, as though they were at once something outside you and an inward state of your own. ... These are things we entrust to you for safekeeping; reveal them only to those who are able to understand.”

This entrusted secret includes the paradox of imamology expressed in the Imam's declaration: if you could see with your own eyes what I possess of the Malakût, you would make me God's equal, whereas I am only a creature. The formula in which the personal pronoun serves as its own predicate—in the second person, anta anta—expresses the condition of the absolute Subject. A subject wholly identical with its predicate needs nothing other than itself to be what it is: it contains no negation and no deficiency.

Qâzî Sa'îd quotes one of the invocations composed by the Fourth Imam (one of the ad'iyat al-sajjâdîya): “My God! How can I call upon You, insofar as I am sufficient unto myself to be myself (anâ anâ)? And how can I keep myself from placing my hope in You, when You are sufficient unto Yourself to be Yourself (anta anta)?”
This means that my own egohood (anâ'îyatî), insofar as it feels itself able to be itself through itself alone, cannot coexist with seeking You, with an invocation addressed to You.

Hence we hear the Imam deny such egohood of himself. Here too we can resolve the dilemma in which literalist theologians have sometimes tried to imprison the imamology of the theosophers. The latter do not begin their metaphysics of being with being as something already there (see § 2 above). They understand its primordial, uncaused coming-into-being as an imperative addressed to being. The fundamental philosophical question is therefore posed not in terms of being (esse) or a being (ens), but as a command: Esto!—“Be!”

Thus there is no longer any question of whether the Imam acts as a demiurgic being to whom divine power has been “delegated” (tafwîd). For the primordial self-creating Will eternally commands being to be, and the Imam-Logos is himself that imperative, that Esto, at every level of his manifestation. The simultaneous presence of lâhût and nâsût, then, will not be understood here in terms of a hypostatic union.

The interlude is brief, but it lets us grasp in a flash how initiation into the Malakût is, by that very fact, initiation into the secret of imamology. Our pilgrims' visionary journey on the White Cloud will now continue. At its fourth great stage they will reach the malakût of the vital reality within humanity. That is why the next episode will again present details like those we have already seen.

III. The Prophet Sâlih. — “Then we came to a garden among the gardens of paradise. And behold, before us was a young man (shâbb) performing the Prayer between two graves. We asked the Imam: ‘Who is this young man?’

“‘He is my brother Sâlih the prophet,’ he told us, ‘and the two graves between which he performs his worship are those of his parents.’ When Sâlih saw us, he approached the Imam in tears. We said to him: ‘Why are you weeping?’ He replied: ‘The Imam used to pass by me each morning and sit with me. My worship grew more fervent as I gazed upon him.

“But he has not come for forty days now, and that has overwhelmed me with sorrow. I cannot hold back my tears of longing for him, because I have suffered the misfortune you see.’ Then we said to the Imam: ‘This is surely the most extraordinary thing we have seen! You were with us every day, and yet every day you came here to visit this knight of the soul (fatâ)?’” (§ 22).

My translation of fatâ as “knight of the soul” is especially significant here. It belongs to a way of thinking that sees the prophets' mission as one of “spiritual chivalry,” their struggle as the struggle of knights. Sâlih, mentioned repeatedly in the Quran, was a nabi, a prophet sent to the Arab people of Thamûd, who, of course, rejected his mission.

Fotowwat (in Persian, javân-mardî) signifies a youthfulness of the soul rather than of the physical person. Its chief virtue is generous, selfless devotion to a cause—here, God's cause. It played a considerable role in Islamic spirituality and, closely bound up with Shiite ideas, gave shape to a way of life governed by the principle of companionship. Others have already suggested “knight” as an equivalent, and it seems to me the best way of conveying what the word implies.

Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's explanation of this episode can be summarized as follows. The Imam now shows his companions the malakût of vital reality, of animate life (hayât hayawânîya, virtus animalis) as it exists in humanity. The “garden of paradise” is here the malakût of that vital reality, containing trees and flowers “planted in animate life,” living creatures carried along in the stream of life.

The young man, the “knight,” who appears as the prophet Sâlih, is the manifest form (mazhar) of the divine Logos or Angel who governs the world of life. As in the case of Khezr, Qâzî Sa'îd declares, in his own terminology, that Sâlih is the throne of the lord of the species of living creatures, the abiding dwelling of the spiritual gift that gives this Logos or divine Word (Kalima rabbânîya) its governing authority.

Among all the divine Names, some possess the privilege of being the Imams of those Names. Each prophet was the manifest form of one of these Imams of the divine Names, until the arrival of the last Prophet, who gathers them all into himself.

Sâlih was the manifest form of the divine Names and Words relating to life; the Angel charged with them is Seraphiel. That is why Sâlih here represents the form in which animate life reveals itself within the human being. It is also why the companions, seeing with their malakûtî gaze, find him alive—unlike Solomon in the next episode, where life is spiritual life in the strict sense, a resurrection brought about by the Imam-Logos.

What, then, are the two graves that Sâlih is digging and between which he performs his worship, his personal liturgy? They are called the “graves of his parents,” meaning the two levels of the plant world and the animal world. “At the level of human reality, these two worlds are indeed buried. For until a human being has died to these two levels of being, he has not yet reached the threshold of human reality, just as, until he has died to the level of human reality, he has not yet reached the level of the superhuman (fawqânîya).”

We might also think, Qâzî Sa'îd remarks, that the two graves represent the two deaths framing the human adventure in this world: death to the other world when we descend into this one, and death to this world at the exitus, our departure back to the other world. There remains the Imam's morning visit to Sâlih.

Sâlih's tears correspond to the falling leaves that, in the preceding episodes and for the same mystical reasons, fell from the withering tree. We need only recall the meaning of the three thirds of the Night explained earlier. Two thirds have already passed—and Sâlih is burying them—the vegetative third and that of the virtus animalis, animate life. The final third belongs to the human being.

And this last third of the Night of matter announces the imminent rising of a sun: not a sun rising in the East, as the physical sun of our world does, but a sun rising in the West, for it marks the appearance of the “day of Resurrection,” which is the “day of the Imam.” Resurrection means precisely this: the sun rising from the West. For whereas the fall into this world is a descent from the East, the spiritual world, resurrection is the return from West to East, to the origin.

That is what the fifth great stage of their visionary journey will mean for the companions, bringing them to the threshold where human reality reaches toward its spiritual, superhuman fulfilment. Their encounter with the prophet Sâlih already implies that chronological time has been enfolded for them. Now, within the Malakût, they will become contemporaries of Solomon's resurrection. Salmân the Pure continues his account.

IV. The Seal of Solomon. — “Then the Imam said to us: ‘Would you like me to show you Solomon, son of David?’ We answered: ‘Certainly!’ The Imam stood up and we rose with him. We walked until we entered an orchard (bostân) unlike anything we had ever seen. It contained every kind of fruit, streams of running water and singing birds. When the birds saw the Imam, they gathered to form a canopy over his head.

“Then we came upon a couch, and on it lay a young man [a ‘knight’], on his back. There was no seal [ring] on his finger. By his head was a serpent, and another lay by his feet. When the two serpents saw the Imam, they coiled themselves at his feet, their faces rolling in the dust of the ground. Then they became like the dust itself” (§ 23).

Here we have a description of the state in which the companions discover Solomon. The following paragraph will show the mystery of Solomon's Seal at work. Naturally, Solomon's condition and the figures around him in the Malakût are full of meaning. The orchard they enter is the human malakût. Because human nature gathers together the natures of plants and animals, its description includes many kinds of fruit and birds.

The fruits are all the theosophical knowledge mystics gather from the tree “which is neither of the East nor of the West” (Quran 24:35). The birds are the “hieratic” souls (in the Neoplatonic sense of the word), taking flight through the space of the spiritual world and the human malakût. “They sing in every variety of their knowledge and mystical perfection; they summon the homesick to the sweetness of the dwelling of intimacy; they kindle in pilgrims the ardent longing to reach the precincts of the supersensible worlds.”

At this mystical station, which the companions have reached through the Imam's spiritual influence and which Qâzî Sa'îd calls the “Lotus of the Boundary” (Quran 53:14), the Imam shows them the Throne of the human malakût in the person of the prophet Solomon. Because Solomon was given “a power belonging to no one after him,” he is the manifestation of humanity's caliphal function: the investiture of the human being as God's vicegerent upon His Earth. This is why spirits and humans, birds and beasts, winds and mountains were placed under Solomon's command.

No one since Gayomarth, the primordial human being of Iranian accounts of human origins, was invested with such a function. Even the Seal of the Prophets chose to be not a king-prophet but a servant-prophet, because the fullness of that caliphal function was to be granted only to his final successor, the last Imam, the Imam of the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat). Why, then, do the companions find Solomon lying on a couch as a young man, apparently stripped of his sovereignty because the mysterious Seal from which that sovereignty comes is missing from his finger?

The companions had seen this Seal in the Imam’s possession at the very beginning of their journey on the White Cloud, when he appeared to them transfigured in his heavenly, theophanic reality. For the Imam is the Seal of absolute walâyat—the inner, spiritual reality of all the prophets and all their prophetic messages. It is therefore he who, by virtue of his cosmic sovereignty, bestows the mysterious power of the Seal upon whomever God wills. Just as the great tree on the mountaintop had appeared withered in his absence, and Sâlih had buried his parents in tears, so here Solomon, deprived of the Imam’s presence, appears deprived of life and power.

As for the two serpents lying at Solomon’s head and feet, their meaning is this. The first represents love of this world, for such love is the source of every error. The other is the serpent of worldly ambition. “There is certainly an indication here,” our commentator writes, “that earthly power is inseparable from these two serpents. This is why the love of power and political ambition bring about the ruin of so many people.”

Yet the arrangement of the figures shows that neither serpent, nor any trace of them, has penetrated Solomon, the prophet of God. And when the Imam appears—the one who is the source and center of all earthly life—the two serpents crumble into dust. At the sudden influx of spiritual power, the false appearances of this world vanish. Salmân the Pure then continues his account, revealing how the mystery of the Seal was disclosed to the companions.

“We said to the Imam: ‘Is that truly Solomon, son of David?’ ‘Yes,’ the Imam replied, ‘and here is his Seal.’ The Imam then removed the Seal from his own finger and placed it on Solomon’s finger. He said to him: ‘Rise, O Solomon, by the power of the One who raises the dead—the God besides whom there is no god, the Eternal, the Living, the Victorious, Lord of my earliest forefathers.’ Then Solomon stood up, and ‘we heard him pronounce the threefold testimony’: to the oneness of God, to the prophetic mission of Muhammad, and to the walâyat of the Imam.” Solomon concluded this threefold testimony by addressing the Imam: “I ask God, my Lord, to count me among your Shiites, for without this I possess nothing and have no power” (§ 24).

The mystery of the Seal therefore involves the folding back of time upon itself. Even before the Imam’s appearance in chronological history, the ancient prophets who preceded Muhammad received from him the Seal that invested them with their authority. Or rather, what appears to us, from the standpoint of chronological time, as a reversal of time is actually the way time unfolds in the “absolutely subtle time” belonging to the Imam’s heavenly reality. This is no longer the time of the Imam’s earthly history but the time of his theophanic person, existing in the suprasensible reality of the Malakût, the spiritual world beyond ordinary sense perception.

The Imam possesses the Seal in his malakûtî reality. When he places that Seal on Solomon’s finger, Solomon becomes alive in the human Malakût. In chronological time, Solomon has been dead for centuries. In the time of the Malakût, Solomon has already risen from the dead, and the Imam’s companions are witnesses and contemporaries of his resurrection. Qâzî Sa'îd insists on a point announced by numerous hadiths: the Imam is the Hand of God.

This means not that he issues commands by his own authority, but that he himself is the divine command that brings the dead to life—the command that is God’s Word. Likewise, as the center of faith, he is at once the Face that the hidden God turns toward humanity and the face that the believer turns toward God. He is therefore the imperishable Face of every being. That is also the meaning of Solomon’s final words: “May God count me among your Shiites; otherwise I have no power.”

Solomon’s power is thus a trace of the Imam’s cosmic sovereignty, and to possess even that trace is, by that very fact, to profess the Shiite faith (tashayyo'). When made sincerely, from the heart, this profession joins the believer to the Imam and to the walâyat of the Imams of the “Family of the Cloak” (âl al-'abâ). This is the complete spiritual assembly—the pleroma—of the twelve Imams of Twelver Shiism, whose lineage begins with those whom the Prophet gathered beneath his cloak on the celebrated occasion when he proposed a trial by divine judgment to the Christians of Najrân.

“This is why,” Qâzî Sa'îd concludes, “a Shiite in the true sense is someone who knows the Imam through the knowledge of light (ma'rifat nûrânîya). Anyone who knows him in another way may perhaps be an adherent, but is not a Shiite in the true sense (shî'î haqîqî).”

The story of the White Cloud thus reveals itself more and more clearly as an initiation into the secret of Shiite spiritual knowledge, whose very heart is the knowledge of the Imam: the Imam as the manifestation of the Complete Human Being (Insân kâmil). The companions’ gradual penetration into Mount Qâf will confirm this. From the multitude of worlds they are about to glimpse, a triumphant hymn of the Imam will arise, proclaiming that the Name revealed in every manifestation of being is itself a manifestation of the Imam as Logos, the divine Word.
Salmân the Pure continues his account:

“We then prepared to make our way around Mount Qâf. I asked the Imam: ‘What lies beyond Mount Qâf?’ He replied: ‘Beyond it are forty worlds, each of them equal to forty times this world.’ We asked: ‘How do you know this?’ The Imam answered: ‘In the same way that I know this world and everything it contains, and that I know the pathways of the Heavens and the Earths’” (§ 25).

Naturally, such a declaration prompts our commentator to explore—or rather, briefly recall—some of the teachings about the creation and structure of the cosmos preserved in Shiite traditions. All concern universes that precede ours in the order of being: suprasensible worlds whose numerical descriptions always carry a symbolic meaning. Foremost among them is a tradition going back to the tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, which speaks of the belt of green emerald surrounding our world. This is the Veil beyond which extend the seventy thousand universes of the Malakût.

The choice of green is never arbitrary. It marks an intermediate state between the world of bodily things, represented by black or blue-black, and the world of the separate Intelligences, represented by yellow. Here Qâzî Sa'îd makes an extended reference to the universe whose mysterious cities are named in a long hadith of the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sâdiq, and in the systematic account of their place in the order of being developed by Suhrawardî: Jâbalqâ in the East, Jâbarsâ in the West, and Hûrqalyâ, their spiritual center.

The commentator also refers to a chapter by Ibn 'Arabî containing perhaps the most beautiful, and at the same time one of the most rigorous, descriptions of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. These worlds are formed of matter in a subtle, luminous state (mâdda latîfa nûrâniya). In itself, such subtle, luminous matter has no fixed dimensions of its own. It is pure receptivity to whatever dimensions, large or small, may actually take form within it.

But as our commentator surveys these traditional accounts of the cosmos, he introduces a digression on the twelve worlds of light. This is another expression of the celebrated hadith of the Twelve Veils of Light, which signify the twelve Imams. We return here to the conversation between the fifth Imam, Muhammad Bâqir, and his disciple Jâbir ibn 'Abdallâh, to which we referred earlier (§ 2, p. 147). In this part of their conversation, the Imam reveals to his disciple the Malakût of the Earths, which was not shown to Abraham. I would like to dwell briefly on this passage.

First, it provides another example of a ritual change of clothing that announces the passage from one world to another, just as it does in the rites of certain mystery religions. Second, as in our story of the White Cloud, it illustrates the meaning of closing or opening the eyes.
